extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy-makers, and grant review administrators interested in NIH R01 peer review, gender bias, and linguistic auditing
extracted.subtask_short: evaluative language in NIH R01 critiques
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and auditing the vocabulary and phrasing used in NIH R01 reviewer critiques to detect gendered evaluative patterns and to inform rubric and process reforms that reduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standout / superlative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of superlative praise words such as 'outstanding', 'exceptional', 'remarkable' to mark an applicant as a top performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts of these terms indicate high praise; the study found male applicants disproportionately receive such 'standout' language. Presence of superlatives can influence downstream scoring and perceptions of brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Words describing personal ability or talent, e.g., 'talented', 'skilled', 'capable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals perceived competence of the PI. The paper treats these as a distinct category from achievement or brilliance; differing use across genders may reflect evaluative bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievement descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that highlight accomplishments or productivity, e.g., 'accomplished', 'productive', 'impressive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on documented outputs and past success. The study notes female applicants are more often described with achievement/productivity language rather than superlatives denoting brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that frames the applicant in terms of future potential, e.g., 'promising', 'potential', 'developing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks expectation of future success rather than current excellence; can function to temporally shift recognition and affect opportunities tied to perceived current standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedging language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of tentative qualifiers such as 'may', 'could', 'appears to' that soften claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates uncertainty and reduces assertiveness of praise or critique; the study found more hedging in critiques of female applicants even when scores were similar, which can undermine perceived competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical language such as 'weak', 'limited', 'concerning' used to flag deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals problems with the proposal or investigator. Frequency and framing of negative descriptors can differentially impact applicants and should be monitored for biased patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to research / project (impersonal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique language that focuses on the research project or aims rather than on the PI personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonal, project-focused references center evaluation on the science; differential rates of project-focused vs person-focused references can reveal bias in how reviews are framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to PI personally (gendered pronouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentions of the principal investigator as an individual, often using gendered pronouns or personal descriptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Person-focused references can emphasize identity or attributes of the PI; such references may introduce gendered language patterns and should be tracked (e.g., more personal commentary for one gender).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to PI's training environment / mentors
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments referring to the PI's institutional environment, training background, or mentors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals contextual evaluation of PI support and scaffolding; may be used differently across genders (e.g., attributing success to mentors rather than PI's independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to team
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that situates the PI as part of a team or emphasizes collaborators rather than PI independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing a PI as a 'team member' rather than an independent investigator can reduce perceived leadership or independence; the study found female PIs more often framed this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male applicants receive more 'standout' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern: male applicants disproportionately receive superlative praise (e.g., 'outstanding', 'exceptional').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern is a measured outcome in the linguistic audit and is implicated in downstream score or opportunity disparities; audits should quantify superlative use by applicant gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female applicants described in terms of competence/productivity rather than brilliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern: critiques of female applicants emphasize achievement/productivity language (e.g., 'productive', 'accomplished') rather than words connoting brilliance or exceptional creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such differential vocabulary can systematically underrecognize exceptionalism and affect career advancement; rubric designers should note that 'achievement' vs 'brilliance' framing matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater hedging in critiques of female applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern: critiques of female PIs contain more hedging language (e.g., 'may', 'could', 'appears to') even when numerical scores are similar to male counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hedging reduces the force of evaluative statements and can disadvantage applicants; monitoring hedging frequency by demographic group is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female PIs framed as team members vs independent investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern: reviewers more often reference female PIs in the context of a team rather than as independent leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing can diminish perceived independence and leadership credentials; review templates or guidance can encourage explicit statements about PI independence when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male PIs described as 'creative' or 'innovative' independently of productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed pattern: male applicants are more often labeled 'creative' or 'innovative', descriptors that connote novelty and intellectual leadership separate from measurable outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative/innovation language elevates perceptions of intellectual contribution; auditing such descriptors can reveal bias not captured by productivity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal critique mediates formal scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: even with the same formal scoring rubric, the language used in written critiques mediates how scores are generated and perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider critique text as an active component influencing scores; reforms should address both numeric rubrics and written narrative guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic auditing of historical critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Method/standard: use algorithmic text mining (e.g., LIWC) combined with qualitative coding to detect biased language patterns in reviewer critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended practice for detecting bias that the formal rubric does not capture; the study demonstrates combining LIWC categories with human qualitative analysis to identify systematic differences by gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train reviewers on language patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention: educate reviewers about language patterns that encode bias and how word choice can shape evaluative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training should highlight examples (e.g., superlatives vs hedging, team-framing vs independence) and encourage neutral, project-focused language where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide structured templates that constrain descriptive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention: use structured critique templates to limit free-form, subjective descriptive language and standardize where evaluative comments belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates can reduce variability introduced by idiosyncratic vocabulary and make critiques easier to audit for biased phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-pass linguistic review before finalizing scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention: perform a follow-up review of submitted critiques to identify and correct biased or inappropriate language prior to score finalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dedicated linguistic check can catch subtle phrasing that may have influenced scores and provide a corrective mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NLP-based bias detection on submitted critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention: deploy automated natural language processing tools to flag potentially biased language in reviewer critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated detection (e.g., LIWC categories, custom classifiers) can scale auditing across large volumes of critiques and highlight candidates for human review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit bias operationalization via vocabulary differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual standard: implicit bias can be operationalized as the systematic use of different vocabularies to describe equivalent achievements across demographic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operationalization links linguistic differences (e.g., 'brilliant' vs 'productive') to measurable downstream impacts and supports using text-based audits to detect bias.
